rows.label: Concept
rows.text: The potentiometer compares emfs, finds internal resistance from two balance lengths, and can be standardised with a standard cell. A smaller potential gradient makes the null more sensitive. Polarity must oppose the wire drop or there is no balance.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: A thermocouple needs a small k.  ·  Do not draw current from a standard cell except at the brief test.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: The applications all use the same null. Comparing two cells uses E1/E2 = l1/l2. Measuring a thermocouple's small emf uses a small potential gradient so that the balance length is long enough to read.  ·  Internal resistance uses two balance lengths. l1 is with the cell alone. l2 is with a known resistance R across the cell, so the cell now sends current and its terminal voltage is smaller. Then r = R (l1/l2 − 1).

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: A standard cell of known emf can set k. If that cell balances at l_s, then k = E_s / l_s, and an unknown balanced at l has E = k l. The standard cell must not be left on load.  ·  Sensitivity improves when k is small, because a small change in emf moves the jockey a long way. That means a long wire or a small driving current, until the galvanometer can no longer see the unbalance.  ·  The wire must stay uniform and at one temperature. A jockey scraped along a hot wire both damages the wire and shifts k.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: l1 is the open-circuit length, the longer one.  ·  The standard cell is not the driving cell.  ·  A smaller k is more sensitive, not less, until detection fails.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: r = R (l1 − l2)/l2, not the reciprocal.  ·  Identify which length is open circuit.  ·  Polarity must oppose.
